items.headline: Rockwood Rocket Tone: 6-Time All-Canadian, and “an Absolute Disaster” as a Sire
items.post_text:
Rockwood Rocket Tone was named All-Canadian six times running. Senior yearling, two-year-old, three-year-old, aged bull. Only two animals in Holstein history ever beat that run.

This was 1949 and the years after, when bull classes still filled the coliseum at the Royal Winter Fair. A champion male could stop traffic on looks alone.

Then his daughters freshened.

E.Y. Morwick, one of the sharpest historians of the breed, needed six words. "A dud, just an absolute disaster." Not as a show bull. As a transmitter.

Andrew Hunt tells the full story in The Bullvine this week, with one number worth keeping. Of the champion bulls of that era, roughly one in six could actually breed.

Those bull classes have since disappeared from the big fairs. The males moved to the sеmen catalogs.

The stage changed. The problem did not. We still weigh what we can see above what we can measure, and the result still lands a season later, on the farm.

When you pick a sire, which of the two is doing more of the work?

#sеmen #cattlebreeding #dairygenetics #holstein

items.headline: Start Where It Hurts: How to Implement Dairy Technology That Scales
items.post_text:
One dairy milked 4,500 cows on two rotary platforms. Its breeding team was ten people per milking.

After installing automated sorting gates, that number dropped to two. Eight people moved to higher-value work. The herd did not shrink. The labor bill did.

Progressive Dairy laid out how this actually happens this week, and the mechanics are worth reading. Sort gates route cows by rule, not by memory. Every cow between 95 and 120 days in milk goes to the hoof trimmer each Wednesday, automatically. Breeding cows and treatment cows separate in a single pass.

The piece makes a quieter point too. The farms that win with technology do not start big. They name their most expensive problem first, missed heats or slow milking or the labor crunch, and solve only that. Then they add one piece at a time, on the same cow IDs.

Most technology is bought before the problem is named. That is the step everyone skips.

What is the one problem you would automate first?

#dairyfarming #precisionlivestock #herdmanagement #agritech
items.summary: The farms that get the most from technology start by naming their most expensive problem – missed heats, slow milking, undetected sick cows or the labor crunch – and solving that first.

items.headline: Many growers still find ‘no meaningful benefit’ from AI use on the farm: survey
items.post_text:
Purdue asked 400 farmers about AI on their operations. More than half, 52%, said the tools provide no meaningful benefit right now.

The detail underneath is sharper than the headline. Agtech usually sells AI as a labor saver. Only 14% of these farmers expected it to cut labor needs or cost. A slightly larger group, 22.8%, thought it would lift production.

Jennifer Marston, writing in AgFunderNews this week, quotes the barometer's lead economist Michael Langemeier. His read is plain. Most respondents simply have not figured out how these tools help their operation yet.

He points to what he calls facts on the ground. A tool can tell you to plant corn on a given day. Weather or a broken machine can make that day impossible.

That last point is the whole story. The barrier is rarely belief in the technology. It is whether the technology survives the conditions of a real working day.

What would it take for a tool to earn a permanent place on your operation?

#agritech #livestock #precisionag #farmtech

items.headline: Holstein’s 60-Inch Rule: Why Breeders Are Backing It With 53%-vs-21% Math
items.summary: Two weeks after the May 2026 stature penalty, breeders answered back with heritability math: 53% vs 21%.
items.post_text:
Two weeks after Holstein USA's new stature penalty landed, docking cows over 60 inches, the sharpest response wasn't outrage. It was a heritability lesson. Andrew Hunt, writing in The Bullvine this week, traces how one comment reframed the debate.

Quebec breeder Emeric Lebacle made the point almost in passing: stature runs about 53% heritable by Lactanet's numbers, while feet and legs sit around 21% for the major score. Push hard on a low-heritability trait and progress crawls. Stature responds roughly 2.5 times more reliably to selection.

The penalty bites gradually: no deduction at 60 inches, minus 0.15 at 61, climbing to minus 3.45 at 70. Taller cows tend to exit the herd earlier, and an early cull costs roughly $2,000 per replacement heifer.

Feet and legs stay weak even in today's top GTPI bulls, and the penalty doesn't fix that directly. A short cow once denied an "Excellent" score became one of Wisconsin's highest lifetime milk producers.

Where would you draw the line between structural durability and chasing a number on paper?

#genetics #Holstein #dairybreeding #heritability #cattlegenetics

items.headline: Increase breeding results with synch protocols and estrus detection aids
items.summary: Latest synchronization protocols and estrus detection aids for greater reproductive success.
items.post_text:
A synchronized cow that never shows heat is a wasted shot. Jordan Thomas, writing in Progressive Cattle this week, breaks down pairing A.I. protocols with estrus detection to catch that before it costs a pregnancy.

The Beef Reproduction Task Force publishes validated protocol sheets each year. For heifers not yet cycling, longer progestin protocols like the 14-day CIDR-prostaglandin give more time to reach puberty. For cows, the classic is 7-day Cosynch plus CIDR, with a newer 7 & 7 Synch variant adding an extra prostaglandin dose.

Thomas flags a real number: half or more of cows can be noncycling at the start of a protocol, especially after a long calving season.

Breeding indicator patches add a decision layer. If 50% or more of the patch ink rubs off, that female is a strong candidate for sexed sеmen. Less than half, and conventional sеmen may be safer.

What's striking is how much depends on what happens before insemination. Detection tells you whether the protocol worked.

Are estrus detection aids underused on your operation, or already standard?

#reproduction #cattlebreeding #ArtificialInsemination #sеmen #dairygenetics

items.headline: Your Oldest Cow Isn't a Cull — She's a $3,000 Heifer You Don't Have to Buy
items.summary: Replacement heifer costs hit $3,010/head, up 164% since 2019, making cow longevity an economic strategy; reproductive health (clearing uterine infections) is one of four pillars keeping cows productive longer.
items.post_text:
A replacement dairy heifer now costs $3,010, up from $1,140 in April 2019. Top auction prices in California and Minnesota have crossed $4,000.

Andrew Hunt, writing in The Bullvine this week, makes the case that keeping an old cow in the herd is no longer sentimental, it is math. The national average is 2.7 lactations. Gillette Emperor Smurf EX-91, a Holstein now in her 18th lactation, has produced 478,163 pounds of milk in her lifetime, a Guinness World Record.

On a 200-cow herd, moving the average from 2.7 to 3.7 lactations saves roughly $60,000 a year, about 20 fewer heifers to raise. USDA counted only 3.914 million replacement heifers on hand this January, the lowest number since 1978.

Hunt names four pillars behind that extra lactation: transition nutrition, udder health, foot care, and reproductive health, specifically clearing uterine infections across consecutive cycles. The fourth pillar is where fertility work quietly pays for itself.

What's the oldest cow still earning her keep in your herd, and what's actually keeping her there?

#reproduction #dairyfarming #cattlebreeding #cowlongevity #dairyeconomics

items.headline: Does delaying conception improve profitability?
items.summary: Study on dry period length and days open: intermediate-length dry periods gave higher milk production and better fertility; questions whether delaying conception in high-producing modern Holsteins improves profitability.
items.post_text:
More than 109,000 Holstein cows. 60 US dairy herds. That is the dataset behind a retrospective study by Overton and Eicker, reported this week by Alvaro Garcia in Progressive Dairy.

The question: does delaying conception pay off in high-producing herds? Modern Holsteins hold their lactation curve longer than cows a generation ago, so some producers wondered if longer days open would squeeze out more milk before pregnancy takes its toll.

The data said otherwise. Longer days open in one lactation raised replacement risk in the next. Dry period length followed a curve, not a line. Both too short and too long raised early-removal risk. Roughly 60 days produced the best outcomes. Cows that conceived earlier and kept a traditional dry period made more milk through 90 days and got pregnant sooner next lactation. Even top producers were not protected once days open ran too long.

Garcia's conclusion: reproductive efficiency is not a pregnancy checkbox. It is a long-term driver of survivability and profit.

Where is your herd's dry period landing right now, and does it match what the cow's transition actually needs?

#dairy #reproduction #cattle #fertility #herdhealth

items.headline: New technology, new possibilities: How to introduce artificial intelligence into your dairy
items.summary: CATTLEytics founder Shari van de Pol explains how AI helps producers with data analytics, breeding schedules, nutrition, disease diagnosis and employee management on dairies of any size.
items.post_text:
"You can have all the information in the world, but if you're not actually making any changes, what's the point?" That is Shari van de Pol, a computer engineer turned large-animal vet, speaking on the Progressive Dairy Podcast in a piece by Patryce Eldredge LeFevre this week.

Van de Pol founded CATTLEytics, an ag-tech company built around one problem: dairies collect enormous data and still struggle to act on it. Her advice is unglamorous. Open ChatGPT, Copilot or Perplexity. Ask a real question about your operation. If the answer feels off, push back and ask it to refine. Start with one problem, not the whole farm.

She is clear about limits too. AI does not replace the nutritionist or the vet. It fills gaps and spots patterns across feed, breeding and health records. Van de Pol also sees it as a leveler, giving smaller operations the kind of analysis only large dairies could previously afford.

The tool is only as useful as the question you bring it. What is the one recurring decision on your operation you would hand to AI first?

#dairy #AI #agtech #dataanalytics #cattle

items.headline: Orbem begins US rollout of MRI-based in-ovo sexing tech
items.summary: German startup Orbem, backed by 55.5M euro Series B, deploys MRI+AI system determining chick sex in-ovo with 99.5% accuracy in under a second; first US hatchery system live, second in mid-August; in-ovo sexing already covers 40% of EU commercial layer flock.
items.post_text:
99.5% accuracy, in under a second. That is the claim behind Orbem's in-ovo sexing system, now running at its first US hatchery, according to AgFunderNews this week.

Orbem is a Munich-founded startup with a Texas office since 2025. Its system, "Genus Focus," pairs an MRI scanner with AI that identifies a chick's developing reproductive organs before hatching, around day 11 to 12 of incubation. A second US installation is scheduled for mid-August, a third for 2027. Jennifer Volz, the company's head of global business development, says a major US retailer will announce its own rollout soon.

The technology is already established in Europe. In-ovo sexing covers 40% of the EU's commercial layer flock. More than 281 million female chicks have been selected this way since 2021. Orbem runs the system as pay-per-use rather than selling hardware, and reports being already profitable after a 55.5 million euro Series B round this January.

Sex determination before birth, at near-perfect accuracy, keeps showing up as the economics driver across species. Where else in animal agriculture is this kind of precision still missing?

#agritech #genetics #AI #innovation #poultry
